This paper presents a novel, to the best of our knowledge, ultra-low latency fronthaul networking approach
based on nanosecond (ns)-precision optical switching with advanced synchronization. We propose and demon-
strate a comprehensive control architecture that integrates precision time protocol (PTP)-based time alignment
with semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA)-based optical switches, enabling coordinated, jitter-minimized
switching with accuracy as fine as 100 ns. Two primary synchronization methods are explored: a distributed
hardware approach employing dedicated timing devices for simultaneous switch configuration, and “SyncNet,” a
software-defined networking (SDN) controller utilizing time information inspired by reverse PTP. Experimental
validation on a commercial Open RAN 5G system shows that our fronthaul switching framework achieves
exceptional reliability, evidenced by only 0.00024% packet loss during link recovery while maintaining steady
throughput (uplink: 1.03 Mbps and downlink: 1.01 Mbps) over repeated switching events. The proposed
architecture supports dynamic reconfiguration for rapid link recovery and energy-efficient, traffic-adaptive
resource allocation. Our results establish a robust foundation for next-generation fronthaul networks, deliver-
ing deterministic performance and flexibility aligned with 6G requirements. This work directly addresses the
escalating needs for ultra-low latency, high reliability, and energy efficiency in emerging mobile and AI-driven

tum, promoting disaggregated network functions and flexible

(CUs) and distributed units (DUs) [7]. This disaggregation
approach enhances openness, interoperability, and vendor
diversity across the RAN, potentially reducing deployment cost
and fostering innovations. However, it also introduces complex
architectural challenges, particularly in the fronthaul segment
connecting DUs and radio units (RUs). While Open RAN
successfully implements Ethernet-based packet transport for

stringent requirements [8]. Fronthaul, the transport segment
between DUs and RUs, carries time-sensitive user-plane and
control-plane information in 5G/6G radio access networks.
This segment is distinct from backhaul and midhaul and is
characterized by much tighter latency, jitter, and synchroniza-
tion constraints—typically requiring nanosecond (ns)-level
timing accuracy. These stringent requirements arise because
fronthaul directly impacts radio signal processing and physical
layer coordination. Even minor timing deviations can degrade
link performance or disrupt service continuity. As networks
evolve toward dynamic and energy-aware architectures, pre-
cise timing and synchronization become critical enablers for
fast reconfiguration and resilience in fronthaul transport.
Currently, most deployments rely on static point-to-point
connections between DUs and RUs due to strict latency and
synchronization requirements under different functional split
options. This static configuration becomes problematic, as
both DU and RU are among the most power-hungry compo-
nents in the RAN infrastructure, with energy consumption
highly correlated with actual traffic load [9,10]. As 6G services
evolve to increasingly dynamic and bursty traffic patterns,
a more flexible fronthaul architecture becomes essential not
only to accommodate traffic variability but also to enable
energy-efficient resource allocation and rapid reconfiguration
in response to changing network conditions for better network
resilience [11]. Current exploration in the telecommunication
industry has been focusing on several switching technologies to
address the growing demands of the fronthaul section in terms
of flexibility and reconfiguration [12]. Conventional Ethernet
switching, while widely deployed for its cost-effectiveness and
simplicity, introduces unpredictable latency variations and
lacks the deterministic performance guarantees necessary for
coordinated network operations in advanced fronthaul scenar-
ios [6]. Flexible Ethernet (FlexE) offers dynamic bandwidth
allocation through layer separation between MAC and PHY
layers, enabling more efficient resource utilization compared
to standard Ethernet [13]. However, FlexE implementation
requires specialized equipment that significantly increases
deployment costs and operational complexity [14]. Based on
a similar concept, time-sensitive networking (TSN) enhances
standard Ethernet with precise timing synchronization and
deterministic packet delivery, achieving microsecond-level
(µs) precision through features such as time-aware sched-
uling and frame preemption. Despite these capabilities,
TSN deployment faces substantial challenges, including the
need for specialized hardware throughout the network and
potential congestion issues affecting high-priority traffic
during peak loads [15]. This electrical solution also requires
optical-electrical-optical (OEO) conversion for any switching
operations. In summary, these electrical Ethernet-based switch-
ing solutions primarily focus on providing flexible, packet-level
connectivity, and bandwidth management, but they rely on
buffering, queuing, and OEO conversions and are therefore
not well suited to forming a deterministic, multi-hop fronthaul
network with real-time, low-latency switching.

enhanced flexibility to support DU migration and improved
resilience for rapid recovery of fronthaul links (including both

based on the precise time protocol (PTP), synchronized fast
optical switches. Our solution encompasses full control of
1 × 4 optical switches with a 10 ns switching time, PTP-based
time synchronization, achieving tracking errors around 30 ns
over several minutes, and a fully manageable, time-aligned
optical switching infrastructure, enabled by “SyncNet,” a
time-aware software-defined networking (SDN) controller.
Leveraging these technologies, we deploy and validate the
proposed fronthaul network using commercially available
Open RAN 5G equipment. Two scenarios are demonstrated:
(1) DU migration triggered by traffic dynamics through on-
demand fronthaul reconfiguration, and (2) fast fronthaul link
recovery, achieving full detection, notification, and restora-
tion within 9.8 µs, with minimal disruption to 5G services.
The integration of fast optical switching with precise timing
control significantly extends the operational capabilities of the
fronthaul. It enables energy-efficient operation and dynamic
adaptability, contributing to a more flexible and resilient RAN
architecture aligned with future 6G requirements.

To improve determinism in Ethernet transport, FlexE
has been proposed as a potential solution for supporting full
packet-based xHaul networks. FlexE introduces converged
client interfaces that support a range of Ethernet MAC rates
and provide increased flexibility for Ethernet-based service
chains. By employing time-division multiplexing (TDM)
calendars within the FlexE shim, bandwidth can be finely allo-
cated across large physical Ethernet links, offering enhanced
isolation between services and support for network slicing
[27]. However, FlexE remains a physical layer management
technology, and the maturity of corresponding switching
mechanisms is still limited. FlexE operates at the physical layer
by creating fixed bandwidth channels over Ethernet links.
Unlike packet-based switching, FlexE switching is currently
limited to static pipe configuration, with minimal flexibility for
scenarios requiring rapid bandwidth reallocation or dynamic
traffic engineering. While it addresses bandwidth isolation and
service convergence, low-latency switching—critical for RAN
fronthaul—is not yet fully supported [13]. In practice, FlexE
calendars are configured on timescales of seconds or longer
and are not intended for sub-millisecond, event-driven switch-
ing of individual fronthaul paths. TSN is another promising
approach that seeks to enable deterministic Ethernet transport
[28]. Originally developed for industrial and internet appli-
cations, TSN has evolved to include enhancements such as
traffic shaping, time-aware scheduling, and standardized time
synchronization [29]. TSN time-aware scheduling can keep
the latency of scheduled high-priority flows in the order of a
few tens of microseconds with bounded jitter, but the sched-
ules are pre-computed and updated on millisecond-or-longer
timescales, which prevents ns- or microsecond-scale recon-
figuration in response to individual failures or DU-migration
events. These electrical packet-switching solutions can only
reconfigure paths when multiple link options are available.
Due to the unpredictable latency and queuing characteristics
of Ethernet switches, implementing multi-hop fronthaul net-
works with these technologies is not yet feasible. Additionally,
these electrical switching solutions face challenges in fronthaul
networking because of the necessary OEO conversions and the
associated management complexity.
In summary, Ethernet technologies such as eCPRI,
FlexE, and TSN can deliver fronthaul streams with end-to-
end one-way network latency on the order of 100 µs and
microsecond-scale jitter when paths are statically engineered,
but their reliance on buffering, pre-configured calendars, and
millisecond-scale control loops means they cannot provide
the real-time (sub-µs to ns-scale) reconfigurability and low-
latency switching required for dynamic DU migration and fast
fronthaul recovery.
B. Optical Switching-Based Solutions for Fronthaul
Networks
Optical switching has gained increasing attention as a prom-
ising solution to bring sub-channel flexibility, inspired by
Google’s recent deployment of optical circuit switching (OCS)
in their tensor processing units (TPUs) [30]. Unlike traditional
electronic switches, optical switches eliminate power-hungry
OEO conversions at intermediate nodes, thereby reducing
energy consumption, latency, and cost; however, they lack
memories for packet-level processing [31]. These properties
make optical switching more suitable for circuit-level switching
in DCNs, as a complement to electrical packet switching sys-
tems [32]. Usually, these applications require optical switches
with switching time at the sub-millisecond level. Fast optical
switches, particularly those based on semiconductor optical
amplifiers (SOAs) [33] and photonic integrated circuits (PICs)
[34], have demonstrated ns-scale switching times. Some initial
explorations in DCNs demonstrated high throughput, flexible
topology reconfiguration, and fine-grained traffic management
Beyond DCNs, several works have explored optical switch-
based architectures in 5G/6G fronthaul. Xu et al . have
reviewed advanced radio-over-fiber interfaces and high-speed
optical links for large-capacity 6G fronthaul, highlighting
wavelength- and sub-channel-granular optical switching as
enablers for scalable, low-latency DU–RU interconnection
[35]. Yang et al . have proposed adaptive time-slot optical
switching for latency-sensitive IoT fronthaul, using time-
division optical switching to guarantee bounded delay for
selected flows [36]. Both approaches demonstrate the potential
of optical switching to support flexible fronthaul connectivity
but rely on microsecond- to millisecond-scale reconfiguration
and scheduled time slots rather than the ns-scale, event-driven
path changes targeted in this work. Recent surveys on optical
x-haul [37] and 6G optical fronthaul [12] further classify these
works as part of a broader move toward reconfigurable optical
transport, while also identifying control-plane scalability,
synchronization, and protection switching as open challenges.
However, bringing fast optical switching into fronthaul
networks introduces new challenges. First, clock management
becomes critical: achieving coordinated ns-level switching
across multiple nodes requires precise time synchronization.
Existing optical switching systems often rely on distributed
timing signals delivered over dedicated links [23], but this
approach is not scalable or robust to dynamic topology changes
and link failures, with much longer coverage in fronthaul
than in typical DCN use cases. The distributed clock with a
dedicated clock channel experiences different delays compared
to the data path, and it lacks the ability to continuously track
these variations. Second, the control plane (SDN controller)
remains a bottleneck to managing multiple optical switches.
Traditional SDN or network orchestration mechanisms are
not equipped to handle the rapid control cycles required for
ns-scale switching. The absence of fast, coordinated con-
trol logic limits the responsiveness and scalability of OCS in
large or highly dynamic environments, such as those antici-

3. PRINCIPLE OF FRONTHAUL NETWORKS
BASED ON FAST OPTICAL SWITCHES
The principle of the proposed fronthaul network is illustrated
in Fig. 1. Instead of relying on fixed point-to-point connec-
tions between RUs and DUs, we introduce a reconfigurable
optical fronthaul network enabled by fast optical switches. This
dynamic fronthaul architecture allows flexible reconfiguration
of interconnections between DUs and RUs, enhancing RAN
operations from two key perspectives. In a fronthaul network,
any RU can connect to the chosen DU through multiple paths,
offering flexibility that surpasses mere reconfigurability.
First, it enables RU traffic migration, whereby multiple RUs
can be aggregated onto a consolidated DU during periods of
low traffic (e.g., at night), reducing overall power consump-
tion at the DU level. When traffic increases, the RU can be
reconfigured with additional DUs to enhance capacity. Second,
the reconfigurable fronthaul introduces link resilience with
available multiple paths, allowing for near-instantaneous recov-
ery from link failures, thereby improving the reliability and
robustness of wireless network services.
These two scenarios—DU consolidation for energy effi-
ciency and rapid recovery from fronthaul failures—are
experimentally validated later in this paper.
However, upgrading from static fronthaul links to a recon-
figurable fronthaul network poses significant challenges,
primarily due to the stringent latency requirements inherent
to fronthaul transport [40]. Conventional Ethernet switches
introduce a fixed forwarding latency in the microsecond range
per hop, but, more critically, their shared buffers can add tens
to hundreds of microseconds of additional, non-deterministic
queuing delay under contention. In multi-hop fronthaul
topologies, this stochastic queuing behavior can easily con-
sume a 100–250 µs latency budget and violate the tight jitter
requirements, even when TSN or FlexE enhancements are
employed. Traditional optical fronthaul deployments based on
CPRI over dedicated fiber or WDM already provide essentially
deterministic, propagation-limited latency and very low jitter,
and therefore meet the timing constraints discussed above.
However, these static point-to-point optical links do not offer
reconfigurable multi-hop networking or energy-aware con-
solidation of RUs and DUs, which are the main targets of this
work. To address this, we adopt ns-scale fast optical switches
that eliminate the need for OEO conversion and enable instant
link configuration under synchronized control. This fast opti-
cal switching approach is key to achieving both the required
latency performance and operational flexibility in future RAN
architectures. The key enabling technologies for fronthaul
networks will be reported in the following chapter.

network, we integrated PTP-based time synchronization
directly into the SDN control plane. A customized controller,
referred to as “SyncNet,” was developed to enable time-aware
coordination of distributed network devices. “SyncNet” deter-
mines the time offset between itself and each control agent

A. Network Reconfiguration
The reconfiguration scenario demonstrates the capability of
the proposed fronthaul network to support dynamic migration
of RUs when they are underutilized or idle, thereby improving
overall energy efficiency in RAN. This is achieved by dynami-
cally switching both uplink and downlink traffic to alternate
optical paths, effectively consolidating active RUs onto fewer
DUs during periods of low traffic demand. The simultaneous
reconfigurations minimized the disturbance to 5G services.
In this scenario, the system performs reconfiguration by
rerouting fronthaul traffic through a predefined recovery
path using 1 × 4 optical switches, while the original primary
path is temporarily freed. The reconfiguration process is care-
fully orchestrated to ensure session continuity and seamless
connectivity, with no packet loss observed during switching
events.
Experimental validation in Fig. 6(a) shows that, following
the manual initiation of RU migration, throughput tempo-
rarily decreases as the system transitions paths. However, the
network rapidly stabilizes, restoring up/downlink transmis-
sion rates to near-baseline levels with minimal fluctuation.
Importantly, the RU–CPE connection remains active through-
out this process without requiring session reinitialization,
confirming the effectiveness of coordinated path switching in
maintaining uninterrupted service.
The oscilloscope traces in Figs. 6(c) and 6(d) presented
the well-defined transmission window and the ns-scale
transition time (10 ns rise time) during link reconfigura-
tion, demonstrating the scheme’s suitability for high-speed
reconfiguration.
This dynamic migration approach underscores the flexibility
of the optical fronthaul architecture to perform energy-aware
resource reallocation, allowing the network to adapt dynami-
cally to traffic patterns by consolidating RUs and reducing
power consumption without compromising reliability or
quality of service.
B. Fronthaul Network Recovery
The network recovery scenario evaluates the fronthaul’s ability
to restore optimal performance after a link failure, focusing on
achieving seamless service continuity with minimal data loss
during automatic rerouting, as represented in Fig. 6(b).
In this use case, downlink recovery is investigated. To verify
the synchronized operations, the coupler in the downlink
is replaced with the other optical switch. Upon detecting a
link failure via the PD on the downlink, the FPGA promptly
signals the SDN controller to initiate an autonomous recovery
procedure. The recovery process is carefully timed using the
PTP-based synchronization framework described in Section 3.
This coordinated switching prevents transient mismatches
in traffic routing that could otherwise cause packet drops or
ordering issues. This procedure involves synchronized recon-
figuration of both optical switches to redirect traffic from
the failed primary path to the protected recovery route. In
Fig. 6(e), the trace for link recovery indicates a total recovery
time of 9.8 µs. This duration encompasses the link power loss,
notification to the SDN controller, and subsequent immediate
reconfiguration.
Traffic throughput and packet delivery were continuously
monitored during recovery using an iperf3 client-server setup
and the MD1230B data quality analyzer, with data traces
precisely time-stamped using the synchronized timing system
for accurate correlation of network events.

Over the recovery interval spanning approximately 80 s,
2,043,059 IPv4 packets were transmitted. Of these, exactly five
packets were lost during the switching window, representing an
exceptionally low packet loss rate of approximately 0.00024%.
A detailed examination of packet capture and timing logs indi-

precise moment of optical path transition—when the switches
simultaneously transitioned links, creating a roughly 10 µs
interruption during which the optical signal briefly dropped
before stabilization, as represented in Fig. 6(e). This minimal
packet loss is validated by correlating the time stamps from
the synchronized control plane with packet sequence num-
bers captured by the analyzer, confirming that all subsequent
packets were delivered successfully once the recovery path was
established. The tight synchronization between uplink and
downlink switching enabled by the PTP-based control frame-
work is critical in confining loss to this brief switching window,
effectively preventing prolonged service disruption.
The measured recovery time in our testbed reflects both
the ultra-fast optical switching and the relatively low latency
between the controller and the agents in a local deployment.
In wide-area networks with higher controller–agent latency,
the same optical switching hardware and synchronization
framework would still provide ns-scale path reconfiguration
once commands arrive, but the overall fault-to-recovery inter-

delays in the control plane. This highlights the importance
of control-plane placement and possibly hierarchical control
architectures when scaling the proposed fronthaul solution
to larger geographical areas. Building on this work, we have
recently integrated an AI-driven control model into the optical
switching framework to further minimize effective downtime.
This model predicts agent–switch communication delays and
proactively adjusts control actions and scheduling, thereby mit-

time and bringing the overall protection behavior closer to the
intrinsic ns-scale capabilities of the optical switches.

protection switching capabilities of the proposed ns opti-

latency-sensitive 5G and future 6G applications requiring
ultra-reliable, low-loss recovery.
C. Discussion on Scalability
Fronthaul networks operate under stricter constraints on
latency, synchronization, and packet loss tolerance. Even minor
packet loss can disrupt PHY-layer functional splits and impact
end-user QoS. In this paper, the experimental validation of
fast optical switching-based fronthaul networks demonstrates
feasibility for small-scale deployments. However, several fac-
tors could limit scalability in larger networks, including the
coordination of numerous optical switches based on precise
timing. Especially, long-distance fiber links and larger node
counts will introduce higher jitter, reducing synchronization
accuracy. Expanding network size also increases the complexity
of the SDN controller, leading to longer reconfiguration times
and slower responsiveness, which will potentially affect the
network recovery time. These limitations can be mitigated by
implementing robust clock synchronization across nodes to
minimize jitter and by adopting distributed SDN controller
architectures to improve efficiency in large-scale deployment.

6. CONCLUSION
This paper presents a synchronization-enabled optical switch-
ing framework for reconfigurable fronthaul networks, with
a focus on improving network resilience and enabling
energy-aware operation. By integrating PTP-based time
synchronization into the control and data planes, we achieved
coordinated ns-level optical switching across distributed nodes,
with measured timing jitter within approximately 100 ns under
hardware-assisted synchronization.
The proposed SDN control architecture supports both
scheduled and on-demand reconfiguration, allowing deter-
ministic switching events to be orchestrated with temporal
precision. System-level validation using a live Open RAN
testbed demonstrated the feasibility of fast fronthaul link
recovery, with minimal disruption to ongoing services. In a
representative recovery scenario, packet loss was limited to
0.00024% across more than two million transmitted packets,
confirming reliable protection switching under fault con-
ditions. Throughout dynamic path transitions, the system
sustained consistent throughput performance—averaging 1.03
(uplink) and 1.01 Mbps (downlink)—while maintaining ser-
vice continuity without session re-initialization. These results
indicate the potential of time-synchronized optical switching
to support emerging fronthaul use cases where reconfigura-
bility and reliability are critical. While further scalability and
integration studies are needed, this work demonstrates a prac-
tical step toward time-aware optical transport in Open RAN
systems and lays a foundation for future 6G infrastructures
requiring low-latency, adaptive networking capabilities.
